description: We’re a two-person team interested in satellite data, AI, and clear ways to explore wildfire history. We’re building an interactive fire calendar that makes MODIS and VIIRS observations comparable. We bring coding and data analysis skills, and welcome teammates with experience in remote sensing, statistics, mapping, or design.
summary:
Orbit & Ember helps people understand when and where fire activity is unusual. Wildfires can destroy homes, disrupt livelihoods, damage ecosystems, and carry harmful smoke far beyond the flames. As climate change brings hotter, drier conditions to many regions, communities need clearer ways to understand changing fire seasons and prepare.

NASA satellites provide decades of fire observations, but their instruments detect fires differently. Combining those records without accounting for these differences can make a new satellite look like a sudden increase in fires. Our app addresses this problem by making the records comparable and testing the results against observations kept separate for validation.

Users choose an area to explore its fire history, understand its usual burning season, and investigate recent satellite detections. Ember, our animated AI guide, explains the patterns with clear answers and supporting graphs, making the information easier to use without specialist knowledge.

Our goal is to help scientists, land managers, and emergency planners recognize unusual conditions, identify periods that deserve closer attention, and prepare with a better understanding of the past.

A rise in recorded fire hotspots can mean more burning. Or it could simply mean that a newer satellite detects smaller fires. Orbit & Ember makes NASA MODIS and VIIRS records comparable so users can investigate changes in fire activity across decades.

Users select a location and time period to understand its usual fire season and identify unusual months. We test our harmonization against observations kept separate for validation, checking whether it preserves seasonal patterns and unusual events while showing uncertainty. This helps scientists, land managers, and emergency planners judge which changes deserve closer attention.

We built the browser application with TypeScript, React, and Vite, using MapLibre and deck.gl for interactive maps and the 3D globe. Its creative approach connects historical analysis with recent satellite detections and Ember, our animated AI guide. Users can ask Ember about a region and receive explanations supported by graphs, making complex records more approachable. The signal network provides alert resources and notification pathways for opted-in contacts.

Throughout development, we considered sensor differences, missing observations, accessibility, and the risk of confusing satellite hotspots with confirmed fires. Our intended impact is to help people investigate changing fire seasons and prepare using clearer, more understandable evidence.
